tldr: In October a paper benchmarked personal agent memory on interaction preferences, asking whether agents stop re-asking what users already told them. In early November, two more benchmarks moved the question from convenience to correctness and security.
whats_new: MemoryDojo (Nov 6) is a benchmark for poisoning attacks through LLM agent memory, where malicious instructions seen in one session can carry into later ones.
why_it_matters: Agent memory is now being evaluated for three distinct failure modes (burdensome re-asking, hallucinated memory, poisoning), so a memory layer needs tests for each, not just recall.

status.detail: Three arXiv benchmarks in about two weeks each probe a different way agent memory can fail.

beats.headline: Benchmarking whether agents remember how users want to interact
beats.summary: Repeated questions, unnecessary confirmations and unwanted outreach framed as interaction burden.

beats.headline: MCPHallu measures reasoning, execution and memory hallucinations in MCP agents
MemoryDojo treats memory as an attack surface

open_questions: Do any agent frameworks or memory products publish results on MemoryDojo?
Do the three benchmarks converge on shared metrics or test harnesses for memory?
Do vendors ship documented mitigations for cross-session memory poisoning?
take_for_builders: If your agent persists memory across sessions, add a test that plants an instruction in one session and checks it is not acted on in the next, and treat stored memory as untrusted input.

day_captions.48ead5cc10a0a69d: Frames memory quality as how often the agent bothers the user again about known preferences.
